newsitem.title: ZAIRE: Hundreds of teenagers enlist with Zaire rebel group.
newsitem.headline: Hundreds of teenagers enlist with Zaire rebel group.

text.p: Hundreds of male teenagers on Saturday responded to an appeal by Zaire's rebels and enlisted at recruitment centres as fighting raged on several fronts of Africa's latest war.
At one of Goma's gendamerie police stations, young men lined up to sign up for the rebel Alliance of Democratic Forces for the Liberation of Congo-Zaire (ADFL).
Outside in the small dusty compound, rebel soldiers kept order as the young recruits queued to board trucks for training centres outside the lakeside rebel capital.
As the recruits scrambled aboard, women in the crowd of onlookers wept.

Chanting slogans against ailing President Mobutu Sese Seko, other bystanders cheered as the smoking trucks, many of them looted in the four-month war, sped off towards Goma airport, which the rebels have turned into a military zone. Goma is on Zaire's eastern border, next to Rwanda.
"Mobutu is a fool, a dangerous snake, we must destroy him," the crowd chanted in unison.
"There were hundreds more (recruits) yesterday," a local policeman told Reuters.

Saturday's enlistment came a day after the Alliance led by veteran Mobutu opponent Laurent Kabila appealed for cash donations and more recruits from the 1,400 km-long (850 miles) stretch of territory they now claim to control.
A communique on rebel radio from their headquarters of Goma appealed for the money to help buy more weapons and combat gear for the rapidly spreading war.
The statement said funds were needed as the ADFL expands its area of control in the war aimed at overthrowing Mobutu -- Africa's longest serving leader.
The rebels have pushed north, west and south over recent days despite a much-touted army counter-offensive.
Kabila's need for troops is being met by rapid training of thousands of young men and women who have enlisted in areas he controls, including former soldiers of Zaire's ragged army.
North of Goma the alliance has fractured and some village warriors, known as Mai-Mai and armed with magic spells as well as guns, have been attacking their former allies.
To the west lie pockets of Hutu soldiers of the exiled former Rwandan army and militias who did not follow at least 700,000 other refugees home in November.
The Hutus, who fled Rwanda in 1994 after the genocide of hundreds of thousands of minority Tutsis, are bitterly opposed to the Alliance, which Zaire says is backed by neighbouring countries.

The ADFL says it gets tiny revenues from exports of hand-dug alluvial gold, coffee and some taxes. The significant income that could come from huge foreign-owned gold concessions in rebel-held territory is not an immediate prospect.
On Thursday, some 5,000 newly trained rebel troops were commissioned by Kabila to join their comrades advancing on several fronts against Mobutu's retreating army.
Mobutu, who seized power in 1965 but bowed to pressure for democratic reform in 1990, returned home on Friday after medical tests in Europe for his prostate cancer and a visit to Morocco.
